passages.t: Chasing the wind, and Jacob at Bethel
passages.happening:
‘Ephraim chases the wind and pursues the east wind all day long’ (verse 1). He multiplies lies and violence. He makes a treaty with Assyria and sends olive oil to Egypt. The LORD also brings a charge against Judah, and he will repay Jacob for his ways (verse 2).

Then Hosea remembers the nation's ancestor. ‘In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel, and in his vigor he wrestled with God’ (verse 3). He struggled with the angel and won, ‘he wept and sought His favor’ (verse 4), and he found God at Bethel and spoke with him there. The LORD, the God of Hosts, is his name (verse 5). ‘But you must return to your God, maintaining love and justice, and always waiting on your God’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Verse 1 describes the double game of Israel's last kings. Menahem paid heavy tribute to Tiglath-pileser III to keep his throne. Later Hoshea, the last king, sent envoys to King So of Egypt hoping for help against Assyria, and was imprisoned for it. Making a treaty with one power while sending olive oil, a valuable gift in diplomacy, to the other was chasing the east wind, the hot, dry desert wind that withered crops and brought nothing good.

The chapter is a covenant lawsuit, and it moves back and forth between Israel's present and its past. The Jacob stories come from Genesis: grasping Esau's heel at birth, wrestling at the Jabbok and receiving the name Israel, and meeting God at Bethel. Hosea's hearers knew them well. The weeping and pleading for favor in verse 4 is not in the Genesis account, and interpreters debate whether Hosea knew a fuller tradition or is interpreting the wrestling, where Jacob would not let go until he received what he asked.

Hosea sets the two side by side. Jacob was a grasper too, but in the end he wept and sought God. Ephraim has his ancestor's cunning without his tears. Verse 6 is the way back: return, keep love and justice, and wait on God.
passages.later: Jacob grasped Esau's heel at birth (Genesis 25:26), wrestled at the Jabbok and was named Israel (Genesis 32:22-32), and met God at Bethel (Genesis 28:10-22; 35:1-15). Micah sums up the same call: ‘to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God’ (Micah 6:8).
passages.asks: Jacob grasped, but in the end he wept and asked. Ask where you are still grasping at what only God can give. And verse 6 joins love, justice and waiting on God. Ask which of the three comes hardest to you.

passages.t: False scales, the prophets, and a flight to Aram
passages.happening:
‘A merchant loves to defraud with dishonest scales in his hands’ (verse 7). Ephraim boasts that he has become rich and that no one can find any sin in all his labors (verse 8). But God has been the LORD his God since Egypt, and he will make them live in tents again, as in the days of the appointed feast (verse 9). He spoke through the prophets, multiplied visions and gave parables through them (verse 10). Is there wickedness in Gilead? It will come to nothing. They sacrifice bulls in Gilgal, and their altars will be heaps of stones in the furrows (verse 11).

Jacob fled to Aram, and Israel worked for a wife, tending sheep (verse 12). ‘But by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved’ (verse 13). Ephraim has provoked bitter anger, and his Lord will leave his bloodguilt on him (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The word rendered merchant is kena'an, which also means Canaan. Canaanites were known as traders, and the word had come to mean merchant. Hosea's choice is pointed: Israel, meant to be different from the Canaanites, has become one in the way it does business, using the dishonest scales the law forbade. Ephraim's boast is that his wealth proves his innocence.

The appointed feast is probably the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israelites lived in shelters to remember the wilderness. God threatens to send them back to tents in earnest. Gilead, east of the Jordan, and Gilgal, near Jericho, both had sanctuaries in Hosea's day, and Gilead was among the first lands Assyria took, about 733 BC. Hosea plays on their names with gallim, heaps of stones.

The chapter pairs two departures. Jacob fled to Aram and served for a wife. Israel was brought out of Egypt by a prophet, Moses, and kept by him. Israel's story was never about its own cunning but about God's rescue through the word he sent.
passages.later: The law forbade dishonest scales (Leviticus 19:35-36; Deuteronomy 25:13-16). Jacob served seven years for Rachel (Genesis 29:20). Moses is called a prophet in the law itself: ‘The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers’ (Deuteronomy 18:15).
passages.asks: Ephraim said his riches proved he had done nothing wrong. Ask where you have treated success as proof that God approves of how you got it. And ask whose word has carried you, as the prophet carried Israel out of Egypt.
